articles.title: Federal officials identify 400 noncitizens registered to vote in Washington state: 'Tip of the iceberg'
articles.summary: Acting U.S. Attorney Neil Floyd told Fox News Digital some noncitizens identified in the probe cast ballots as many as 27 times, with alleged votes dating back to 1984.
articles.body: The Department of Justice (DOJ) announced Monday that investigators have identified more than 400 noncitizens illegally registered to vote in Washington state, some of whom have cast ballots in multiple elections dating back decades. Many on the list are green card holders with legal immigration status and permanent residency, according to the U.S. attorney’s offices for the Eastern and Western districts of Washington. "We have identified over 400 noncitizens who are registered to vote and have voted in multiple elections. This is only the tip of the iceberg," Neil Floyd, acting U.S. attorney for the Western District of Washington, said in a statement. "We will continue to investigate and identify those who are committing crimes by voting illegally." DOJ HAS VERIFIED 20,000 NONCITIZENS ON CALIFORNIA VOTER ROLLS, FEDERAL PROSECUTOR SAYS The move builds on the DOJ's legal action against Los Angeles County, where it has sought to set aside roughly 20,000 mail-in ballots sent to individuals whose citizenship status is in question. Immigration officials told Fox News Digital Tuesday that dozens of noncitizens have also been arrested nationwide in a major voter fraud crackdown. In an interview with Fox News Digital, Floyd said investigators identified hundreds of noncitizen voters by reviewing U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) records, which showed that some people who applied for certain benefits had also voted. While some individuals voted only once or three times in past elections, Floyd said others voted as many as 27 times. In total, his office counted approximately 1,500 instances of noncitizens casting ballots. He emphasized that some noncitizens had been voting for decades, predating Washington’s transition to a vote-by-mail system. "I think the earliest moment we have is 1984," Floyd said. "It's early ‘90s, late ’80s, I believe." However, Floyd said he had not checked whether any of the individuals voted in the upcoming midterms, explaining that he did not want to "interfere with the current election." The number of potential noncitizen voters could represent only a fraction of the broader population, Floyd said, because the list includes only individuals who sought certain benefits in Washington state. NINTH CIRCUIT QUESTIONS TRUMP DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST TO SET ASIDE 20,000 CALIFORNIA MAIL BALLOTS "If you take that population, and you expand it out to include all the people that are here illegally that we haven't had contact with, just my estimation is that it's going to be in the thousands," Floyd said. Federal officials said many green card holders were registered to vote without their knowledge through Washington’s Motor Voter program, which integrates voter registration into the state’s Department of Licensing. "We have heard from green card holders who were registered against their knowledge via the Washington Motor Voter program. Then they receive a ballot in the mail and assume they are legally registered — that simply is not the case," the notice said. According to the Washington secretary of state’s website, eligible residents are automatically registered to vote only if they provide proof of U.S. citizenship during a driver’s license or ID card registration process. The findings have prompted federal officials to identify patterns in how the voter registration process has failed, Floyd said. According to the DOJ notice, federal officials are asking Washington state to set aside ballots cast by the identified individuals until their citizenship status can otherwise be confirmed. "Washington is now on notice that noncitizens are voting. It is up to the state to take action to make sure that they are not allowing these noncitizens to vote illegally," the notice said. Officials warned that voting as a noncitizen can have serious consequences for those seeking to become U.S. citizens. Potential criminal charges include making false statements in a naturalization application, and some individuals could also face charges for fraudulent voter registration. On Tuesday, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) told Fox News Digital numerous illegal aliens had also admitted to unlawfully registering to vote or casting ballots in U.S. elections. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Of the dozens of suspects arrested, at least 18 had voted in a federal election. The individuals were from a range of countries, including Mexico, Somalia, Honduras, Guyana, Cuba, Germany, Nicaragua, Venezuela, Vietnam, El Salvador, Cambodia, Guatemala, Portugal and Italy. Many also faced charges for numerous alleged crimes, including counterfeiting, fraud, kidnapping, DUI, sexual offenses, assault with a dangerous weapon, drug possession and burglary.

articles.title: Judge finds L.A.'s top federal prosecutor is unlawfully serving, bars him from two cases
articles.summary: The judge barred Bill Essayli from overseeing two prosecutions but delayed the order's effect, leaving his leadership of the L.A. office under a legal cloud.
articles.body:
A federal judge on Tuesday ruled that Bill Essayli is unlawfully serving as Los Angeles' top federal prosecutor and ordered him disqualified from overseeing two criminal cases, rejecting the Justice Department's latest effort to preserve his authority.

Senior U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright, however, delayed the disqualifications from taking effect while he considers an anticipated government request for a stay pending appeal.

Although the order applies to two prosecutions, Seabright rejected the legal arrangement that has allowed Essayli to continue leading the office under the title of first assistant U.S. attorney. He concluded that the Justice Department had unlawfully delegated powers so sweeping that Essayli in effect occupied the U.S. attorney's position.

"In sum, Essayli is unlawfully serving as a 'de facto' United States Attorney," Seabright wrote.

After learning about Seabright's ruling from The Times, Essayli on Tuesday afternoon said that his office expected it and that the case "will be decided by the Supreme Court." In a follow-up email, he said, "I look forward to serving in my current role until then."

H. Dean Steward, a defense attorney who filed a renewed motion in August challenging Essayli's authority, called the decision "a victory for the rule of law and the U.S. Constitution."

"The Trump administration ignored the laws governing the appointment of U.S. Attorneys and got caught in Los Angeles," he said in an emailed statement. "Trump and his Department of Justice violated the law again and again in an effort to install minions as chief federal prosecutors."

The dispute is part of a nationwide battle over the Trump administration's efforts to install its chosen prosecutors without Senate confirmation. Alina Habba stepped down as New Jersey's top federal prosecutor in December after an appeals court found her appointment unlawful. In Virginia, a judge's finding that Lindsey Halligan was unlawfully appointed led to the dismissal of indictments against former FBI Director James Comey and New York Atty. Gen. Letitia James.

In his Tuesday ruling, Seabright declined to dismiss the indictments against defendants in the two cases that he banned Essayli from overseeing. Jaime Hector Ramirez and Tu Anh Tran had not shown the substantial prejudice required for that relief, he said in response to attorneys' requests to dismiss the indictments. His order bars Essayli from participating in or supervising their cases, including overseeing the attorneys handling them.

Seabright last year ruled that Essayli was "not lawfully serving" as acting U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, but allowed him to continue exercising authority as a special attorney and first assistant U.S. attorney.

The new decision follows a U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruling rejecting a similar arrangement for Nevada prosecutor Sigal Chattah. The appellate court ruled that the Department of Justice cannot keep an official who has not been confirmed by the Senate in charge of a U.S. attorney's office simply by giving that person a different title and the full powers of the job.

The Trump administration has asked the U.S. Supreme Court to review the Nevada decision, arguing that federal law allows the attorney general to delegate a vacant office's powers and install a new first assistant as its acting leader. The Supreme Court has not said whether it will take up the case.

The Justice Department sought to address the 9th Circuit ruling through a revised delegation of authority expressly excluding certain powers reserved for a U.S. attorney. At an Oct. 13 hearing, Assistant U.S. Atty. Alexander Robbins argued before Seabright that the revised delegation placed Essayli's authority on the permissible side of the line drawn by the appeals court.

Seabright found that the revision made no meaningful difference because those powers could not have been delegated to Essayli in the first place.

"Withholding the three specific statutory powers mentioned in the revised designation order in reality withholds nothing," Seabright wrote.

A former Republican member of the California Assembly from Riverside, Essayli has used his position to act as one of Trump's fiercest legal foot soldiers. He has pursued criminal charges against protesters, activists and immigrants while dropping cases involving administration allies and supporting lawsuits challenging transgender and environmental policies in California.

Essayli was sworn in as interim U.S. attorney in April 2025. Around the time he hit that role's 120-day limit, he resigned and then-Atty. Gen. Pam Bondi appointed him as a special attorney and designated him first assistant in an attempt to make him acting U.S. attorney.

Seabright rejected that maneuver last year. But the judge initially permitted him to supervise prosecutions in his other roles — an arrangement the subsequent 9th Circuit ruling undermined.

Trump still had not nominated anyone to serve as U.S. attorney for the Central District of California as of Tuesday's ruling, Seabright noted.

At the Oct. 13 hearing, Robbins said the government would appeal any disqualification ruling and warned of "the chaotic practical effects" of an order taking effect without a stay.

Under the schedule accepted by Seabright, prosecutors have five business days after the ruling to seek a stay pending appeal. If he denies that request, the disqualifications would take effect one week later, subject to further orders from him or an appellate court.

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Murkowski backs Alaska Democrat for governor
articles.summary: Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) endorsed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in Alaska’s governor’s race Tuesday, crossing party lines to back the former state lawmaker over three Republican candidates. In a statement released by Kreiss-Tomkins’ campaign, Murkowski praised the Democrat for his commitment to bipartisanship, arguing that Alaska needs a governor willing to work with lawmakers from both…
articles.body:
Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) endorsed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins in Alaska’s governor’s race Tuesday, crossing party lines to back the former state lawmaker over three Republican candidates.

In a statement released by Kreiss-Tomkins’ campaign, Murkowski praised the Democrat for his commitment to bipartisanship, arguing that Alaska needs a governor willing to work with lawmakers from both parties.

“Our future is too important to be hamstrung by partisan divisions,” Murkowski said. “Jonathan understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face.”

In an interview with Alaska News Source , Murkowski ripped outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s (R) administration for failing to take advantage of federal funding opportunities.

“I have found fault with the Dunleavy administration,” she said. I think that they have left federal money on the table. I think in certain areas, where we have worked hard to put opportunities from the federal side, here, into the state, the state has failed with it.”

Kreiss-Tomkins, who represented Sitka and surrounding communities in the state House for a decade, has campaigned on bipartisan cooperation. He pledged to include Republicans and independents in his administration if elected.

“I’m honored to have Senator Murkowski’s support,” he said in a statement. “Alaskans deserve a government that can work through disagreements and make progress on the issues that matter.”

The endorsement comes just a week before Election Day, where Kreiss-Tomkins leads a four-way race to replace the term-limited Dunleavy. A September New York Times/Siena poll found Kreiss-Tomkins leading with 40 percent support among likely voters, followed by Bernadette Wilson (R) at 20 percent, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson (R) at 15 percent and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor (R) at 11 percent.

President Trump, a critic of ranked-choice voting , endorsed Wilson earlier this month and has urged Bronson and Taylor to drop out of the race to avoid splitting the Republican vote.

Trump has repeatedly attacked Murkowski for crossing party lines, calling her the “Republicans’ Worst Senator” and a “DISGRACE to Alaska and our Country” in a recent Truth Social post.

Murkowski, who has frequently broken with her party, previously endorsed former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) in her unsuccessful 2024 reelection bid. She is backing Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) in his reelection campaign against Peltola this year.

articles.title: Federal grand jury declines to indict Cassidy Hutchinson
articles.summary: A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday rejected the Justice Department’s attempt to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her testimony to lawmakers about President Trump’s actions during the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol. Justice Department attorney Neville Hedley told U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that the grand jury…
articles.body:
A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday rejected the Justice Department’s attempt to indict former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her testimony to lawmakers about President Trump’s actions during the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the Capitol.

Justice Department attorney Neville Hedley told U.S. Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui that the grand jury had not concurred on the proposed charges, though he did not specify the defendant. People familiar with the situation told The Washington Post that Hedley, who identified himself as the acting senior litigation counsel, was referring to Hutchinson.

The Hill has reached out to the DOJ for comment.

The decision marks another setback for the Trump administration’s efforts to pursue criminal charges against the president’s political adversaries.

Hutchinson, a former aide to Trump’s onetime White House chief of staff Mark Meadows, became a key witness in the House investigation into the Capitol attack. She testified in June 2022 about the president’s actions leading up to the riot.

She told lawmakers that Trump allegedly knew some of his supporters were armed when he encouraged them to march to the Capitol as Congress gathered to certify former President Biden’s 2020 election victory.

Hutchinson also testified that she had been told Trump lunged toward a Secret Service agent and attempted to grab the steering wheel of his presidential vehicle after learning he would not be taken to the Capitol.

The former aide acknowledged that she was not a witness to the incident herself, and her account was later disputed by Secret Service personnel.

Trump and his allies have repeatedly accused Hutchinson of lying to Congress during her testimony.

Earlier this year, Reps. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) and Barry Loudermilk (R-Ga.) referred Hutchinson to the DOJ for potential prosecution, alleging that she provided false testimony to the congressional committee.

In an unusual move, the investigation was handled by the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, led by Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon.

Some federal prosecutors had privately expressed doubts about the strength of the case against Hutchinson and whether a conviction could be secured, The New York Times reported.

Grand juries rarely reject proposed indictments because prosecutors only need to convince a majority of jurors that a crime occurred, a substantially lower standard than the proof required for a conviction.

articles.title: Trump reups calls to put Cruz on Supreme Court in vacancy scenario
articles.summary: President Trump joked Tuesday that Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) would be his pick for the next Supreme Court vacancy, saying the senator could get unanimously confirmed because lawmakers in both parties would jump at the chance to get rid of him in Congress. During a midterm rally in Lubbock, Texas, the president praised Cruz as…
articles.body:
President Trump joked Tuesday that Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) would be his pick for the next Supreme Court vacancy, saying the senator could get unanimously confirmed because lawmakers in both parties would jump at the chance to get rid of him in Congress.

During a midterm rally in Lubbock, Texas, the president praised Cruz as a “brilliant lawyer” before suggesting he had found a way around the often-contentious Supreme Court confirmation process.

“I picked three Supreme Court justices, and it’s very hard to get them approved,” Trump said, referring to his appointments of Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett. “I said, ‘Look, I have an answer to it.’ Ted is a brilliant guy, brilliant lawyer, brilliant all that,” he said.

Trump continued, “Went to law school, top student, everything, top credentials. I said, ‘I have an answer to not being able to get it past the Democrats or the Republicans together.’ I would pick Ted Cruz to be the next Supreme Court justice.”

Trump predicted that in an unusual move, Democrats would “100 percent” support the nomination because “they hate the guy and they want to get rid of him.”

“And the Republicans would 100 percent vote for it because they can’t stand him,” he continued. “They would like to get rid of him. So I’d get 100 percent of the vote, and he would be a Supreme Court justice, and he’d do a great job.”

The president has repeatedly floated Cruz as a potential Supreme Court pick, often using the prospect of his nomination to poke fun at the Texas Republican’s complex relationships with his Senate colleagues.

He made a similar joke earlier this year during a White House event in July promoting Trump Accounts, suggesting Cruz’s departure from the Senate would be one of the few things Democrats and Republicans could agree on.

Cruz, however, has made it clear he has no plans to trade his Senate seat for a lifetime appointment to the nation’s highest court.

At an April event hosted by The Wall Street Journal, Cruz said Trump has spoken to him “seriously” about filling a hypothetical vacancy, but said his priority is policy fights rather than legal battles.

“In the first Trump term, the president spoke to me seriously about all three vacancies, and three times I said no, because I don’t want to be out of the arena of the political battle,” Cruz said during a Wall Street Journal Opinion Live interview.

Trump is heading to San Antonio, Texas, for a campaign event in support of Republican U.S. Senate candidate Ken Paxton and Rep. Carlos De La Cruz (R-Texas).

articles.title: Trump and Talarico hold dueling Texas rallies
articles.summary: President Trump and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) shared their competing visions Tuesday as the two held dueling rallies in the Lone Star State one week before the midterm elections. Trump did two rallies in Texas — the first in Corpus Christi and another in Lubbock. It’s his fourth trip to Texas to support…
articles.body:
President Trump and Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) shared their competing visions Tuesday as the two held dueling rallies in the Lone Star State one week before the midterm elections.

Trump did two rallies in Texas — the first in Corpus Christi and another in Lubbock . It’s his fourth trip to Texas to support Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

Talarico held his own rally in Lubbock on Tuesday. He was in Corpus Christi on Saturday.

The Texas race is one of the most contested and watched Senate races in the country. Talarico and Paxton remain close in the polls — Real Clear Polling calls the race a toss-up, with Talarico holding a slight lead.

A Democrat winning the Senate seat would be a shock — none have won a U.S. Senate race in Texas since 1988, and Trump won the state by nearly 14 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election.

Democrats are vying to take control of the House and the Senate. The party would need to win four seats to win control of the Senate.

The president started off his rally in Corpus Christi saying that Texans would defeat “Democrat Communist James Talafreako,” using the nickname he’s given to the candidate.

At both rallies, Trump criticized Talarico on a range of issues like immigration, the Second Amendment and barbecue.

“If you’re running in Texas and if you don’t like guns, and if you don’t like meat and if you don’t like oil, I think you should be losing by a lot,” Trump said at the first rally about Talarico. “Where the hell did they get this guy?”

Trump spoke heavily about the Venezuelan oil tanker that arrived in Texas on Tuesday that is carrying oil to be refined in the state. He said that Talarico would try to take it away.

“Talafreako stated that he wants to dismantle Texas oil and gas and capitalism itself. He wants to take it apart,” Trump continued, adding that Talarico will “kill millions of Texas jobs.”

In Lubbock, Trump said Talarico “wants to get rid of your guns. He wants to get rid of your oil. Wants to get rid of your meat. He can’t stand the stuff.”

Talarico has denied being vegan and said he supports the Second Amendment, but advocates for gun control.

Talarico, for his part, thanked Texans for showing up for his rally in Lubbock, just three miles away from Trump’s, invoking Trump’s nickname for him.

“That’s a lot of Talafreakos in one room,” he said.

He said Texans are “ready for change” and hit the Trump administration over the Iran war and tariffs.

“Change that will roll back these corrupt tariffs that are raising grocery prices. Change that will end this corrupt war in the Middle East, driving up gas prices,” he said. “We are done with the extremism and the corruption. We’re done with the politics of division, and we are ready for something new.”

The Democratic Texan hit on Paxton, calling him the “most corrupt politician in Texas.”

“Ken Paxton is everything that’s wrong with our politics,” he said. “He doesn’t serve us. He serves himself.”

“Ken has spent his entire career enriching himself and his donors. I’ve spent my career working with both parties to cut your property taxes, lower your housing costs, and capping your insulin copays,” Talarico continued. “I have a legislative record. Ken Paxton has a criminal record.”

Paxton has never been convicted of a crime, though he has faced criminal indictments, federal investigations and impeachment while serving as the state’s attorney general, but he was acquitted.

Talarico compared Paxton to “that one guy” at a Texas bar.

“He’s loud. He’s obnoxious. He makes everybody feel uncomfortable. He hears you say your name to the bartender and then adds his drink to your tab when you’re not looking,” he said. “That’s Ken Paxton. And I don’t know about y’all, but I am done picking up his tab.”

“This isn’t a partisan thing,” he continued. “Republicans know just as well as Democrats that there is no place for guys like Ken Paxton in Texas.”

articles.title: GOP Sen. Lisa Murkowski endorses Democratic candidate in Alaska governor’s race
articles.summary: The Republican senator endorsed Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins over Trump-backed Bernadette Wilson a week before Election Day.
articles.body: Sen. Lisa Murkowski endorsed the Democratic candidate for governor in her home state of Alaska on Tuesday, snubbing GOP contenders who include a Trump-backed candidate a week out from Election Day. Murkowski, one of President Donald Trump’s more vocal critics among Senate Republicans, said she is backing Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins over Bernadette Wilson, who has Trump’s endorsement. “JKT is a young Alaskan with a view and a perspective that I think Alaska needs right now — a freshness of energy, a commonsense guy who has a known ability to be working together,” she said in an interview on NBC affiliate KTUU of Anchorage. Murkowski said she believes the three Republican gubernatorial candidates on the ballot in Alaska, which has ranked choice voting, are too partisan. “We need a governor who’s going to work with the Legislature,” she said. “That has got to happen for the delegation to be successful back in Washington, D.C.” Kreiss-Tompkins, a former state lawmaker, told KTUU he was grateful for Murkowski’s support. “I have a lot of respect for Lisa, her integrity. I think she’s worked across the aisle in Congress, which is a quality I really admire and hope to live up to if I’m elected governor,” he said. “And I’m very grateful that she wanted to step up and be a part of the coalition that we’re building.” He added that the two of them have “had a few conversations” as his campaign has progressed, “and I think she just got to a degree where she felt she was confident in our ticket and our ability to solve problems for Alaska.” In the race to succeed term-limited GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy, Kreiss-Tomkins is competing with former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson, former state Attorney General Treg Taylor and Wilson, whom Trump endorsed this month. The NBC News Decision Desk rates the governor’s race in Alaska, where Trump won in 2016, 2020 and 2024, as leaning Democratic. In her comments to KTUU, Murkowski raised concerns that Wilson wouldn’t work at any point with Democrats. Wilson was dismissive of her endorsement. “Given that Senator Lisa Murkowski abandoned Alaska values a long time ago, I am not surprised that she has endorsed ‘Just Keep Taxing’ JKT,” she said in a statement, arguing that Kreiss-Tomkins’ “allegiance lies with extreme socialists hellbent on fighting President Trump to the detriment of everyday Alaskans.” Murkowski, who isn’t up for re-election until 2028, endorsed GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan in his re-election bid this year. He is in a competitive race that includes a candidate named Dan J. Sullivan Jr. and Democratic candidate Mary Peltola. The Trump administration sued election officials in Alaska last week, arguing that Sullivan Jr.’s appearance on the ballot could mislead voters who intended to support Sullivan’s re-election. Murkowski criticized the move, writing on X, “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot.” Trump tore into Murkowski the next day on social media, calling her the “Republicans’ Worst Senator, by far.”

articles.title: James Talarico faces off against Trump in dueling Texas rallies in election’s final days
articles.summary: Voter enthusiasm in Lubbock, a Texas city of fewer than 300,000, underscored the stakes of a close Senate race in what Democrats call their best chance in a generation.
articles.body: LUBBOCK, Texas — On the day a sitting president landed in their town for the first time in 34 years, people waited for hours in lines that stretched for blocks in this reliably red city. But this crowd on the east side of the city wasn’t waiting for President Donald Trump. They wanted to see Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico. “We’re all closet Democrats,” said Dr. Tim Jones, 66, an emergency room physician, laughing and gesturing to a sea of people around him in line before Talarico’s evening rally. “There are a lot of people who are finally upset at gas prices, diesel prices, inflation, lies, the war, all of it. It’s the corruption, tearing down part of the White House to build this vanity ballroom. I mean, it’s just pathetic. So people finally are deciding, ‘We’ll get out to vote.’” Less than 3 miles away, a similar scene unfolded for Trump, who held a rally at the expansive Lubbock Memorial Civic Center as he sought to boost the Republican Senate candidate, state Attorney General Ken Paxton. In a new move, Trump brought out his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, who won one of the biggest rounds of applause of everyone Trump introduced. The dueling rallies and the fount of voter enthusiasm in this city of fewer than 300,000 underscored the high stakes in a Senate race that has drawn hundreds of millions of dollars in spending and presents the biggest threat in years to the Republican Party’s grip on bright-red Texas. With just a week until the election, Talarico has held a narrow lead in polling. His trip to Republican turf is a sign he is trying to win Republican crossover votes he needs for a victory. At their rally Tuesday, Democrats urged supporters to seize a once-in-a-generation chance to flip a statewide seat after three decades of Republican control. They panned the economy, high gas prices and closures of rural hospitals. Talarico repeatedly cast Paxton as corrupt and as a Trump sycophant. He called out Elon Musk, saying the tech billionaire — who has significant business interests in Texas — is trying to buy his own personal senator after having thrown more than $150 million into Paxton’s candidacy. “We have an affordability crisis because we have a corruption crisis. But we can change that in this election, in this state, in this race,” Talarico said. “We are running against the embodiment of this corrupt system. We are running against the most corrupt politician in Texas.” Republicans, meanwhile, showcased Trump, who cast Talarico as a Second Amendment-hating, meat-loathing extremist out of touch with everyday Texans. Minutes into his speech, Trump referred to him derisively as “Talafreako.” He mentioned Talarico’s disappearance from the campaign trail earlier in the month, when he said he had the flu. Trump said he believed the reason either was a “mental problem” or he was “sick to his stomach” from eating meat. While there are far more Republicans in Texas than Democrats, Republican strategists say they view the contest as a real fight at a moment when Americans are feeling anger and dissatisfaction toward Washington. Paxton has also battled his own personal scandals, creating a drag on his numbers. And Texas Republicans are still beset by infighting after a nasty primary campaign, when Trump endorsed Paxton over Sen. John Cornyn, who had the backing of much of the party’s establishment. Paxton has leaned on Trump’s advocacy. Trump has visited Texas three times this month, holding a pair of rallies Tuesday. “Is it not awesome and amazing to be onstage with the greatest president in my lifetime?” Paxton told the crowd as Trump stood behind him and looked on. Paxton said he spent the day with Trump, starting with a campaign stop in Corpus Christi. He said that as they were arriving in Lubbock, Trump told him he doesn’t normally do two rallies for any candidate: “He said, ‘I must really like you.’” “Mr. President, I really like you, too,” Paxton said. In a potential sign that Republicans were looking to attract a greater cross-section of voters, Trump handed Rubio a speaking part at the rally, as he did earlier in the day in Corpus Christi. Rubio has generally held higher approval ratings than others in the administration, including Trump. He is also a possible candidate in the 2028 presidential election. Rubio, who had stayed clear of midterm campaign rallies until Tuesday, took the microphone and kept it brief. “Our enemies are weaker. Our country is stronger, and our people are safer because Donald J. Trump is the president of the United States,” he said at the Lubbock rally. Trump called Talarico an “anti-gun extremist” and said he and Paxton are the only things standing between Talarico’s becoming a senator. “They’ve got a lot of bad people,” Trump said of Democrats. “That’s why we can’t afford to lose to some freak.” But Talarico has embraced the moniker, calling out that he had never seen so many “Talafreakos” packed into one room. “Lubbock is ready for change,” he declared to deafening screams. More than 4,000 people signed up to attend the event Tuesday night, according to his campaign. “They are scared. They are terrified. They see what we see — that we’re about to win this election.”

images.caption: Trump gave out hats at his rally in Lubbock on Tuesday. Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty
Democrats hope Talarico can help them win a Senate seat that has been in Republican control for decades. Kaylee Greenlee / Reuters

articles.title: Federal judge rules Bill Essayli unlawfully serving as de facto US attorney in California
articles.summary: Bill Essayli says the Supreme Court will ultimately decide his fate after a federal judge ruled he is unlawfully serving as a de facto U.S. attorney.
articles.body: A federal judge has disqualified Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor in Southern California, from overseeing two criminal cases after finding that he is unlawfully serving as a "de facto" U.S. attorney. U.S. District Judge J. Michael Seabright ruled Tuesday that Essayli cannot participate in or supervise the prosecutions in the two criminal cases. However, the disqualification will not take effect immediately, giving the Justice Department time to seek a stay pending appeal. "We respectfully disagree with the court's order," Essayli said in a statement provided to Fox News. APPEALS COURT RULES TRUMP ADMIN UNLAWFULLY APPOINTED NEVADA'S TOP FEDERAL PROSECUTOR "The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department," Essayli continued, adding that "ultimately, this question will be decided by the Supreme Court, and I look forward to serving in my current role until then." Essayli originally served as interim U.S. attorney under an appointment that expired after 120 days. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi subsequently appointed him as a special attorney and designated him first assistant U.S. attorney. He was never formally nominated by the president or confirmed by the U.S. Senate. Seabright previously found that the arrangement did not lawfully make Essayli acting U.S. attorney but allowed him to continue supervising prosecutions under his other titles. BLANCHE SURVIVES REPUBLICAN DEFECTORS AS TRUMP GETS HIS NEW ATTORNEY GENERAL However, after the Ninth Circuit ruled over the summer against a similar arrangement involving a federal prosecutor in Nevada, Seabright decided to revisit the issue, according to the Los Angeles Times. Attorney General Todd Blanche issued a revised designation last month to narrow Essayli's authority and distinguish his situation from the Nevada case, but Seabright ruled the modified arrangement still gave Essayli enough authority to effectively occupy the vacant U.S. attorney position. "In sum, Essayli is unlawfully serving as a 'de facto' United States Attorney," Seabright wrote. The ruling came as Essayli has been helping lead a high-profile Justice Department effort challenging California over more than 20,000 registered voters the administration says are likely noncitizens. NINTH CIRCUIT QUESTIONS TRUMP DOJ'S EMERGENCY REQUEST TO SET ASIDE 20,000 CALIFORNIA MAIL BALLOTS The Justice Department has asked a federal court to require ballots associated with those individuals to be separated while their eligibility is reviewed, and U.S. District Judge David O. Carter said he would issue a ruling Wednesday on the administration's request. "I think this case is really on the forefront of the administration's battle to fight for election integrity," Essayli said during a news conference Tuesday. "We wanna stop illegal voting. We don't wanna chase it later," he added. When asked about Seabright's ruling during the news conference, Essayli gave reporters a brief response.
